note.text: A bank provides deposit and payment services and extends credit. It brings financial relationships together, assesses borrowers and manages risks, rather than merely storing every customer’s deposit as labelled notes. A customer’s deposit is a claim on the bank. A loan granted by the bank is its claim on the borrower. Liquidity concerns meeting payments when due; credit risk concerns failure to repay. These can interact but are not the same. The lesson describes economic functions without recommending any institution or announcing account rules.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain deposit-taking, payments and lending while distinguishing liquidity and credit risk. Builds on: money forms, desired balances and real value. Leads to: commercial-bank functions and the bank balance sheet.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: An imaginary bank serves a Bamenda trader receiving deposits and paying suppliers. Another customer borrows for a stated purpose. The bank must consider repayment and settlement needs. A sound-looking loan may not be immediately convertible into cash for a payment; a failed borrower may reduce the value of the bank’s assets.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify who owes whom. Separate a deposit claim, a loan claim and a payment service. Ask whether a difficulty concerns timing of liquid funds or loss from non-repayment. Do not infer that a profitable-looking bank can ignore payment needs.

example: deposit-taking: accepting balances owed by the bank to customers.
